common_name: Pink Double Delight Coneflower (AAS-Winning Double Pink Echinacea)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery transplants after frost danger passes, into well-drained soil in full sun; Pink Double Delight was bred to flower reliably the first year from seed and won an All-America Selections award for that trait.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Pink Double Delight produces fully double, rounded blooms in which the central cone is replaced by a tuft of shaggy rose-pink petaloids surrounded by a single ring of flat guard petals, an unusual pompom form among coneflowers that are normally grown from seed rather than division. It was recognized with an All-America Selections award for its ability to bloom heavily in its first season when started early indoors, a trait many perennial coneflowers lack. Keep soil on the lean, well-drained side, since overly rich or soggy ground shortens the life of double-flowered cultivars, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Secret Love Coneflower (Double Rose-Pink Hybrid Echinacea)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Secret Love is part of a compact, heavily double-flowered breeding line developed to hold its shaggy pompom blooms upright on sturdy stems.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Secret Love bears fully double, rounded rose-pink flowers in which the central cone disappears beneath a dense tuft of petaloids, giving each bloom a soft, ruffled pompom look quite different from the flat single daisies of wild purple coneflower. Its compact, well-branched habit holds the heavy double flowers upright without flopping, an improvement over some older double coneflower lines. Site it in sharply drained soil, since double-flowered Echinacea selections are more prone to crown rot in heavy, wet soils than the species, and divide crowded clumps in spring every few years to keep plants vigorous.

common_name: Secret Affair Coneflower (Double Lavender-Pink Hybrid Echinacea)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Secret Affair carries large, fully double lavender-pink flowers on a compact, well-branched plant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Secret Affair produces large, fully double flowers with a dense, shaggy mound of lavender-pink petaloids in place of the cone, fading to a slightly paler mauve-pink at the tips of the surrounding guard petals, giving each bloom a soft, two-toned glow. The sturdy, compact plant branches freely and carries flowers well above the foliage through most of the summer. As with other heavily double coneflower selections, sharp drainage and lean soil help it persist longer than it would in rich, wet ground, and dividing congested clumps every few years keeps the planting vigorous.

common_name: Flame Thrower Coneflower (Bicolor Orange and Gold Echinacea)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Flame Thrower bears single, bicolor flowers that shift from deep orange at the base of each ray petal to golden yellow at the tip.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Flame Thrower stands out among hybrid coneflowers for its bold, two-tone single flowers, with each slightly drooping ray petal glowing deep orange near the coppery-brown center cone and shading outward to bright golden yellow at the tip, a sunset effect unlike the solid-color blooms of most Echinacea. It flowers over a long season from early summer into fall and, being a single-flowered type, offers pollinators easier access to pollen and nectar than the double pompom cultivars bred from the same hybrid lines. Give it sharp drainage and avoid heavy, wet winter soil, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain bloom quality.

common_name: Pixie Meadowbrite Coneflower (Compact Dwarf Rosy-Pink Echinacea)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pixie Meadowbrite is a dwarf coneflower selection bred for a compact habit well under two feet tall, suited to small gardens and container plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Pixie Meadowbrite is a dwarf hybrid coneflower bred specifically for small-space gardens, forming a tidy, dense mound well under two feet tall that still produces abundant single, rosy-pink, slightly drooping daisy flowers around a coppery cone through most of the summer. Its compact scale suits the front of a sunny border, a raised bed, or a large container, where a full-sized coneflower would quickly overwhelm its neighbors. It attracts bees and butterflies through the bloom season and goldfinches feed on the seed heads if left standing into fall and winter; divide congested clumps every few years to keep the dwarf habit tidy.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Pink Poodle Coneflower (Double Pink Pompom Echinacea)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pink Poodle produces fully double, curled pink flowers with no visible cone, carried on a sturdy, well-branched plant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Pink Poodle earns its name from dense, fully double flowers in which curled, candy-pink petaloids almost entirely obscure the central cone, producing a fluffy, rounded bloom quite unlike the flat single daisies of the species. The sturdy, well-branched plant carries its shaggy pompom flowers well through summer, making it a conversation piece in a mixed border or cutting garden. Because double-flowered coneflower selections are more prone to crown rot than the species, give it sharp drainage and avoid overly rich, wet soil, and divide congested clumps every few years to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Jindai Tatarian Aster (Compact Sturdy-Stemmed Fall Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Jindai is a notably compact, sturdy-stemmed selection of Tatarian aster that stays far shorter than the species and does not require staking.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Jindai is a Japanese-origin selection of Tatarian aster prized for its noticeably more compact, upright habit and thick, rigid stems that hold a flattened cluster of small lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers high above the foliage without flopping or needing support, a significant improvement over the tall, sometimes leggy wild species. Its large, coarse-textured basal leaves give it a bold presence even before the late-fall bloom, and the sturdy clumps slowly expand by rhizomes into substantial colonies at the back of a border or along a pond edge. Cut stems back in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every several years to maintain vigor.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Fulgida Coneflower (Southeastern Coastal Plain Orange Coneflower)

planting.note: Direct sow or set out divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this is the nominate wild variety of orange coneflower, restricted to the southeastern coastal plain and distinct from the more widely cultivated var. sullivantii that produced 'Goldsturm'.

directions: This southeastern coastal plain variety of orange coneflower is the nominate type variety, narrower-leaved and generally shorter than the widespread var. sullivantii that gave rise to the ubiquitous 'Goldsturm' cultivar, and it occurs naturally in moist pine savannas, ditches, and seasonally damp meadows from the Carolinas into the Gulf states. It bears the same golden-yellow, dark-coned daisy flowers from mid to late summer, drawing native bees, butterflies, and skippers, with seed heads that feed goldfinches into winter if left standing. Grow it where a slightly more delicate, naturalistic look is wanted than the robust horticultural selections offer, such as a regional wildflower meadow or rain garden margin, and divide crowded clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Little Henry Rudbeckia (Dwarf Quilled-Petal Sweet Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Little Henry is a compact sport of 'Henry Eilers' discovered for its shorter stature, keeping the same unusual quilled petals on a plant roughly half the height.

directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun. Little Henry is a naturally occurring compact sport of the native sweet coneflower selection 'Henry Eilers', retaining the same distinctive golden ray petals rolled into narrow quills rather than the flat form typical of Rudbeckia, but on a plant that tops out at roughly half the height of its tall parent and needs no staking. Its anise-scented foliage and sturdy, well-branched habit make it a better fit for small gardens and the middle of a mixed border than the towering original, while still blooming heavily from late summer into fall and providing nectar for pollinators and seed for goldfinches. It tolerates average to moist soil better than many drought-adapted Rudbeckia, suiting it to a rain garden edge as well as a standard bed. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
